title: Israel queued, Europe saved, and the barrels moved.

pages.title: A queue is a vote of confidence

a-queue-is-a-vote-of-confidence.title: A queue is a vote of confidence
a-queue-is-a-vote-of-confidence.dek: Israelis voted in record numbers by mid-afternoon. Both camps read the same turnout figure as a threat and a reason to hurry. Tonight's first numbers will be estimates; the habit worth keeping is to wait for the count.
a-queue-is-a-vote-of-confidence.text: By 16:00 local time, 15:00 in Berlin, 55.7% of Israel’s eligible voters had cast a ballot, just over four million people [1]. The Central Elections Committee said that was the highest figure at that hour on its books; at the same point in 2022 it was 47.5% [1]. The records had been falling all day: 31.5% by noon, the highest at that hour in 53 years, and 44.9% by 14:00, about 3.29 million ballots [2]. Desk arithmetic: 55.7 minus 47.5 is 8.2 percentage points ahead of 2022 at the same hour, and the gap widened at every reading the committee published [3]. One figure, two fears. Watch what the campaigns did with that number. Benjamin Netanyahu told right-wing voters to “race to the polls”, warned of high turnout in Arab and left-wing areas and claimed “they are trying to steal the election from us”, pointing to three Ra’am activists arrested on suspicion of bribing voters [1]. Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar answered that the prime minister was laying the groundwork to contest the result, and told its own voters the margin “must be enormous” [1]. The committee said it had found no evidence of systematic tampering and was handling individual reports as they came in [1]. This is the old behavioural loop of election days. A turnout figure is neutral; it does not say who voted. Yet each camp reads the other’s queue as a threat, and the threat becomes the reason to join the queue. Fear is a cheap mobiliser. It also leaves a residue: voters primed all day to expect theft are slower to accept a count that disappoints them. The dull machinery did its job. The more useful story is the committee’s. Faced with lengthening lines, it changed its guidance so that polling officials could begin identifying the next voter while the current one was still behind the booth, and it made clear that anyone who arrives by 22:00 will be able to vote [2]. Not everyone had a smooth day. Haaretz and the Arab legal aid group Adalah relayed reports of waits of several hours and slow identity checks in Bedouin towns in the Negev and in Arab communities in the Galilee [1]. Those reports are now on the record, where complaints belong, rather than in a speech. What you will see tonight, and how to read it. Israel has had a poll blackout since Friday night: no new poll results could be published until the stations close [3]. At 22:00 local, 21:00 CET, the television channels release exit polls, which are estimates from samples of voters, not results [3]. In 2022 the three main channels’ first exit polls gave the right-religious bloc 61 or 62 seats; it won 64 [3]. Meretz was given four or five seats by all three and finished below the threshold with none [3]. Soldiers’ and other double-envelope ballots are counted later at the Knesset, and official results are due by 4 November [3]. Why does that matter? Because the first number sticks. In a Brennan Center experiment with 1,994 US registered voters, showing a candidate with 84% odds on a betting market raised the share who thought that candidate would win by 20 percentage points, whatever the polls said [4]. And a warning to be cautious about the odds made no difference to how much people relied on them [4]. Scepticism, in other words, is not a shield. A habit is. The habit is boring and it works: treat tonight’s 21:00 figures as a forecast for a count that has not happened yet, and notice when a politician tells you the result before the committee does. And give the queue its due. People do not stand for hours to post a ballot into a system they think is rigged. Whatever the speeches said today, four million votes by mid-afternoon are four million small acts of trust in an envelope, a ballot box and a count. That trust is the institution’s best asset. The way to keep it is to let the slow part, the counting, finish.

oil-on-paper-rose-oil-in-hand-fell-15.title: Oil on paper rose, oil in hand fell $15
oil-on-paper-rose-oil-in-hand-fell-15.dek: Middle East crude exports are back above pre-war levels, Hormuz carries about 82% of its old flow, and the physical barrel has got cheaper. The futures market still prices the next attack.
oil-on-paper-rose-oil-in-hand-fell-15.text: This morning the count was ships at anchor. This evening it is barrels that got through. Middle East crude exports have averaged 17.3 million barrels a day so far in October, up from 16.4 million in September and above the 16.9 million of the two months before the war, according to Kpler data cited by Reuters [1]. The strait is working, slowly and expensively. Crude flows through Hormuz reached 11.7 million barrels a day in October, about 82% of pre-war levels, against less than 1 million in April, excluding Iranian oil, Kpler says [1]. More tankers sail in convoys along Oman’s coast under US naval protection; about a third of crossings still use the Iran-controlled northern route, Reuters reports [1]. This happens under fire: 28 attacks on commercial shipping were confirmed or reported this month, the highest monthly tally in the Washington Institute’s tracking [1]. Two prices for one barrel. Dated Brent, the benchmark for physical cargoes, has fallen about $15 in under two weeks to some $120, while Brent futures gained about $10, Bloomberg reports [1]. On Tuesday afternoon futures were down 1.7% at $113.88 [2]. The physical market is pricing what is available. The futures market is pricing what might happen next: Iran’s supreme leader said on Tuesday that the state of “neither war nor peace” needs to end, and discussed keeping “control” over the strait [2]. The quiet signal. The premium of the nearest Dubai contract over the following month has shrunk to under $1 a barrel from about $15 a month ago [1]. Desk arithmetic: the cost of wanting oil now rather than in a month has fallen by more than nine tenths. Buyers have stopped bidding as if supply might vanish tomorrow. For you, the barrel that matters is the physical one: it is what refiners actually buy. Freight, convoys and storage are how an economy reroutes itself around a war, one invoice at a time.

neither-war-nor-peace-and-a-supreme-lead.title: "Neither war nor peace", and a supreme leader who wants it over
neither-war-nor-peace-and-a-supreme-lead.dek: Iran's leader met his security chief to discuss conditions for ending the war. Control of the strait was on the list. Washington is weighing a deal or more strikes.
neither-war-nor-peace-and-a-supreme-lead.text: Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei met Mohsen Rezaei, his top national security official, to discuss the Islamic Republic’s conditions for ending the war with the United States, according to a post on the supreme leader’s account cited by CNBC [1]. The current state of “neither war nor peace” needs to end, he said, and the two discussed “safeguarding national and regional security by maintaining control” over the Strait of Hormuz [1]. Diplomacy, in layers. On Monday Saudi Arabia’s defence minister held direct talks with President Masoud Pezeshkian in Tehran, with senior military and intelligence officials from Pakistan and Turkey present [1]. Qatar’s representatives travelled to Tehran on Sunday, Reuters reported [1]. Tehran described the talks as a step towards regional security cooperation, with further consultations possible, according to the state outlet Tasnim [1]. The other half of the table. President Donald Trump told Fox News on Sunday that he was approaching a decision on whether to strike a deal with Iran or intensify military operations [1]. Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia continued over the weekend [1]. The market’s verdict was modest: Brent futures fell 1.7% to $113.88 by 16:10 CET, a second day of losses [1]. Earlier in the day they had been down 1% at $114.74 [2]. A leader saying a war should end is not a treaty. But conditions are what treaties are made of, and someone has started listing them.

1-4-million-a-day-to-move-a-supertanker.title: $1.4 million a day to move a supertanker
1-4-million-a-day-to-move-a-supertanker.dek: Freight is the war's quietest tax. Gulf producers have started paying part of it themselves.
1-4-million-a-day-to-move-a-supertanker.text: Benchmark earnings for very large crude carriers from the Middle East to China are nearing $1.4 million a day, more than 12 times pre-war levels, according to Reuters [1]. Freight has eased from its peaks, but the cost still squeezes refining margins and pushes producers to offer discounts, Bloomberg reports [1]. The response is a change in contracts, not in speeches: Aramco and Adnoc have started selling some cargoes delivered to China and India, taking on shipping arrangements that buyers would normally handle [1]. Eleven supertankers were damaged this month alone, more than 30 since the war began [1]. A seller who pays for the voyage is a seller who wants to keep the customer. That is how trade survives a war: one contract clause at a time.

hsbc-met-on-profit-and-still-fell-7-per-.title: HSBC met on profit and still fell 7%
hsbc-met-on-profit-and-still-fell-7-per-.dek: Europe's largest bank missed on revenue, not on profit, and its shares touched a six-month low. Around it, a drugmaker, a packaging firm and a chip-equipment maker raised the numbers that matter. The index barely moved.
hsbc-met-on-profit-and-still-fell-7-per-.text: HSBC’s shares fell nearly 7% on Tuesday and touched a six-month low, after third-quarter revenue missed estimates, partly because its wealth business grew more slowly [1]. Pretax profit was in line with expectations [2]. The bank index fell 1.1% and the FTSE 100 0.8% in the morning; the STOXX 600 was down 0.1% at 640.07 by 10:20 CET [1]. By early afternoon it had edged up 0.1% [2]. Why a bank can earn and still disappoint. “Banks have been the winners of the latest quarter before this one,” said Ipek Ozkardeskaya of Swissquote Bank, but “short-term yields rising more than long term” is “eating into the income revenue” [2]. That is the dull machinery behind the headline: a bank borrows short and lends long, and when the short end climbs faster, the margin narrows. No scandal, just arithmetic. The rest of the ledger was better. Novartis raised its full-year guidance for core operating income and rose 1.7% [1]. SIG Group, which makes packaging, jumped 9.4% after lifting its margin guidance [1]. BE Semiconductor rose 8.5% after Applied Materials said it had raised its stake in the Dutch maker of chip-packaging equipment to 20% [1]. “The earnings results, generally speaking, have been pretty solid,” said Richard Flax of Moneyfarm [1]. France, the quiet weight. French consumer confidence fell five points to 80 in October, its lowest since June 2013, as student protests spread to unions [1]. French shares were flat after falling more than 2% last week [1]. For you, the lesson of the day is that one large company can move a headline and very little else. Results season is a long queue of invoices being added up: more than a third of S&P 500 companies report this week [2]. Nothing here is investment advice.

orders-up-1-8-per-cent-confidence-at-91-.title: Orders up 1.8%, confidence at 91.7, and Coca-Cola raised its forecast
orders-up-1-8-per-cent-confidence-at-91-.dek: While Europe watched one bank, America published its receipts. They were better than expected, and the ten-year sat at 5%.
orders-up-1-8-per-cent-confidence-at-91-.text: Three US releases arrived on Tuesday and all three beat the consensus. Durable goods orders rose 1.8% in September, against an expected 1.7% [1]. New home sales were 676,000, down 0.6% from August but above the 653,000 economists polled by Dow Jones had pencilled in [1]. Consumer confidence rose to 91.7 in October, against an estimate of 81.0 [1]. The companies said the same, mostly. Coca-Cola and United Parcel Service, a bellwether for the economy, raised their forecasts, Reuters reports [2]. Hilton and JetBlue showed the other side: rising costs from the Middle East conflict [2]. More than a third of S&P 500 companies report this week [2]. That is the useful kind of noise: hundreds of firms adding up what they sold and what it cost. The bond market took note. The ten-year Treasury yield rose to 5.003% and the two-year to 4.741% as the Fed’s two-day meeting began [1]. Fed funds futures price about a 90% chance of a hold on Wednesday, according to the CME FedWatch Tool [1]. Good news on spending is, for a central bank fighting inflation, a reason not to hurry. Desk arithmetic: consumer confidence came in 10.7 points above the estimate. Surveys can surprise; invoices settle the argument later. The Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, PCE, is due on Thursday [1]. Nothing here is investment advice.

gold-at-4-010-the-euro-near-its-may-low.title: Gold at $4,010, the euro near its May low
gold-at-4-010-the-euro-near-its-may-low.dek: Two quiet prices on a busy Tuesday, both waiting for three central banks.
gold-at-4-010-the-euro-near-its-may-low.text: Spot gold eased 0.1% to $4,010.96 an ounce on Tuesday, Reuters reports [1]. The euro slipped 0.2% to $1.114, near the May low it touched two weeks ago [1]. Neither moved much, and that is the information: markets are waiting for the Fed on Wednesday, the ECB on Thursday and the Bank of Japan, all three expected to hold [1]. “We remain medium-term bullish on the ‘picks and shovels’ trade,” said Mohit Kumar of Jefferies, while admitting that “a number of companies will not remain profitable and even go bust” [1]. A forecast that names its own losers is more honest than most. Nothing here is investment advice.

serbia-a-majority-without-a-name-and-a-c.title: Serbia: a majority without a name, and a calendar
serbia-a-majority-without-a-name-and-a-c.dek: The Student List won 140 of 250 seats with no prime minister picked. The constitution now sets the pace: 30 days to a parliament, 90 more to a government, a president by 27 December.
serbia-a-majority-without-a-name-and-a-c.text: Serbia’s Republic Electoral Commission has put numbers on Sunday’s upset. On preliminary results from 8,187 polling stations, the Student List won 2,267,615 votes, 52.71%, and 140 seats; Aleksandar Vučić’s United Serbia list won 39.17% and 104 seats [1]. About 4.3 million people voted [1]. Turnout was 68.78%, the highest in more than 30 years, according to the commission’s Sunday figures [2]. A majority needs 126 of the 250 seats [2]. Desk arithmetic: 140 seats is 14 more than a majority, so the winners need no coalition partner. What the movement does not yet have is a name at the top. It ran deliberately without a hierarchy and named no candidate for prime minister [2][3]. Ilija Srdanović, the Novi Sad cardiologist who headed the list, is widely seen as the likeliest choice, but the ministries of interior, finance and justice are open [2]. One Belgrade analyst told the Guardian the movement’s decision-making also needed to “be sped up”, since choosing candidates “took a long time – months” [3]. The constitution will help with that. The new National Assembly must meet within 30 days of the final result; a government must be formed within 90 days after that [2][3]. Separately, because Vučić resigned as president on 27 September, Ana Brnabić, the assembly’s president and acting head of state, must call a presidential election by 27 December [2]. The programme is institutional rather than rhetorical: an independent police unit answerable to prosecutors, a ban on appointing party loyalists to state companies, and independent scrutiny of large infrastructure contracts [3]. Those are dull promises, which is their virtue. They will be tested in public institutions staffed, as the Guardian puts it, with civil servants loyal to the outgoing regime [3]. A movement born of a collapsed railway canopy in Novi Sad now has to show that procedure, not personality, can carry a country.

ankara-s-committee-signs-off-the-mecca-p.title: Ankara's committee signs off the Mecca pact; the floor vote comes next
ankara-s-committee-signs-off-the-mecca-p.dek: Turkey's foreign affairs committee approved the joint defence agreement with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan. The other two have already ratified it.
ankara-s-committee-signs-off-the-mecca-p.text: The Turkish parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee on Tuesday approved the bill to ratify the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement between Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan [1]. The pact was signed in Mecca on 7 August by President Erdoğan, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif; Saudi Arabia and Pakistan have completed their own ratification [1]. It treats an attack on one as an attack on all three [2]. Deputy Foreign Minister Levent Gümrükçü told the committee the agreement was “entirely defensive” and “envisions integration rather than bloc-building” [1]. It provides for regular consultations, joint training and exercises, defence-industry co-production and technology sharing [1]. The committee chairman, Fuat Oktay, answered the obvious question: was this an alternative to NATO? “Absolutely not,” he said [1]. The timing gives the paperwork weight. Since the Houthis stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia this month, neither Türkiye nor Pakistan has announced strikes on the group, and on Monday the Saudi defence minister, Pakistan’s army chief and Türkiye’s intelligence chief were in Tehran trying to calm things [2]. What you are watching, then, is a parliament doing the slow part. A treaty signed by leaders in August becomes binding only when legislators have read it, questioned a minister and voted. That is the order things should happen in, and it is happening in that order.

wisconsin-a-20-000-cap-and-35-million-th.title: Wisconsin: a $20,000 cap, and $35 million through the party
wisconsin-a-20-000-cap-and-35-million-th.dek: Campaign filings show three donors gave 92% of one governor candidate's quarterly money, routed legally through the state party.
wisconsin-a-20-000-cap-and-35-million-th.text: A week before the US midterms, the Brennan Center has read the end-of-September filings in four close governor races [1]. In Wisconsin, three donors, Diane Hendricks and Richard and Liz Uihlein, accounted for 92% of Republican Tom Tiffany’s fundraising in the prior quarter [1]. State law caps individual gifts to statewide candidates at $20,000 but not gifts to parties, which may pass on unlimited sums: the three gave nearly $60 million to the state Republican Party, which transferred nearly $35 million to Tiffany [1]. Democrat David Crowley has raised about $12 million, $3 million of it from his party [1]. The Brennan Center calls the party route a loophole; it is a legal one, and the cap and the exemption are both Wisconsin law [1]. The useful fact is that you can see it at all, because the filings are public.

kindness-to-yourself-works-through-flexi.title: Kindness to yourself works through flexibility
kindness-to-yourself-works-through-flexi.dek: A study of 318 Turkish adults finds that self-compassion goes with fewer depressive symptoms, and that much of the link runs through the ability to think flexibly.
kindness-to-yourself-works-through-flexi.text: Researchers at Sakarya University surveyed 318 adults aged 18 to 65 and published the results in Frontiers in Psychology [1]. People who treated themselves with more kindness reported fewer depressive symptoms; in a simple model, self-compassion accounted for roughly 32% of the variation in depression scores [1]. The interesting part is the route. The authors tested two possible pathways at once: unconditional self-acceptance, valuing yourself without needing success or approval, and cognitive flexibility, the ability to reinterpret a bad experience and find another response [1]. Flexibility carried the clearer share of the link; self-acceptance showed only a weaker indirect effect [1]. Self-compassion kept a direct link of its own even with both in the model [1]. Read it with the brakes on. It is one survey at one point in time, so it shows association, not cause; it is just as possible that feeling less low makes people kinder to themselves [1]. The sample was recruited online, was 76% female and highly educated [1]. The authors call for longitudinal and experimental studies, and say that training programmes built on these skills remain a hypothesis to test [1]. Still, the finding points somewhere practical. Flexibility is a skill, not a temperament. You cannot order yourself to feel better, but you can ask a second question about a bad day: what else could this mean? The study suggests that the habit of asking may be where self-kindness does its work.

eight-per-cent-ask-the-machine-about-the.title: Eight per cent ask the machine about the midterms
eight-per-cent-ask-the-machine-about-the.dek: A Pew survey finds few Americans use AI chatbots for election information. Those who do mostly want to check what they have heard.
eight-per-cent-ask-the-machine-about-the.text: About half of US adults now use AI chatbots, but only 8% say they are using them for information about this year’s elections, according to a Pew Research Center survey of 5,273 adults taken from 12 to 18 October [1]. Among those who do, 76% look up where candidates stand, 71% check the accuracy of something they heard or read elsewhere, and 40% ask for suggestions on how to vote [1]. Use is higher under 50 (11%) than over 50 (4%) [1]. The reassuring detail is the second figure: most people who ask a machine about an election are fact-checking, not outsourcing the choice. The question for the tools is whether their answers are worth checking against.

wednesday-s-power-is-249-and-lignite-is-.title: Wednesday's power is €249, and lignite is back at work
wednesday-s-power-is-249-and-lignite-is-.dek: The auction for Wednesday cleared at €249.21 per megawatt hour, the dearest day since mid-September. The plants that sat out the storm weekend have returned, and even the cheapest hour now costs €190.
wednesday-s-power-is-249-and-lignite-is-.text: This morning’s piece called Tuesday’s €155 the end of the storm discount. The midday auction has since priced Wednesday, and the answer is steeper. The German-Luxembourg day-ahead price for delivery on Wednesday 28 October averages €249.21 per megawatt hour, according to SMARD, the Bundesnetzagentur’s data portal [1]. That is the highest daily average since 14 September, when it reached €256.55 [1]. Desk arithmetic: Wednesday costs about 61% more than Tuesday’s €155.11 and a little over twice Monday’s €116.57. No cheap hour left. On Tuesday the midday hour, 12:00 to 13:00 CET, cleared at €43.50 [1]. On Wednesday the cheapest hour, 13:00 to 14:00 CET, clears at €189.91, and the dearest, 18:00 to 19:00 CET, at €343.09 [1]. Desk arithmetic: the evening peak is now about 1.8 times the cheapest hour, against six times on Tuesday. The spread narrowed because the floor rose, not because the evening got cheaper. Who came back. The storm weekend showed what the system does when wind is plentiful: it switches off its oldest fuel. Lignite plants generated 54,346 megawatt hours on Saturday 24 October, the lowest day since 14 June, and 62,470 MWh on Sunday [1]. By Monday they were back at 162,086 MWh [1]. Desk arithmetic: lignite output roughly tripled in two days. The month in brown coal. The weekend dip hides the longer line. From 1 to 26 October lignite plants generated about 5,592 gigawatt hours, against about 4,932 GWh on the same days of 2025 [1]. Desk arithmetic: about 13% more this October. A dear gas market makes the old coal blocks competitive again, and the carbon bill follows. None of this is a failure of the market. A price of €343 at 18:00 is a loud, public signal to anyone with a battery, a flexible factory shift or an interconnector to sell into. The answer to a still, dark evening is not a speech. It is storage that charged when Sunday’s wind was nearly free. Nothing here is investment advice.

moscow-writes-a-declaration-buyers-read-.title: Moscow writes a declaration; buyers read the contracts
moscow-writes-a-declaration-buyers-read-.dek: The Gas Exporting Countries Forum adopted a Moscow Declaration on Tuesday. The host asked for long-term contracts and crisis consultations among exporters.
moscow-writes-a-declaration-buyers-read-.text: The eighth summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum ended in Moscow on Tuesday with the adoption of a Moscow Declaration, according to the Kremlin’s record of the plenary session [1]. Around the table sat, among others, Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian and Algeria’s prime minister, Sifi Ghrieb [1]. The host’s figures. Vladimir Putin told the session that forum members account for 70% of the world’s natural gas reserves and around 40% of global exports [1]. He said global gas consumption grew by 1.2% last year to 4.2 trillion cubic metres, and cited a projection of 5.5 trillion cubic metres a year by the middle of the century [1]. The host’s asks. He proposed expanding consultations within the forum on responding to crises in the gas market, including physical threats to infrastructure, and pointed to OPEC Plus as a model of cooperation on the oil side [1]. He argued that investment “must be underpinned primarily by long-term contracts” [1]. He also said prices “could fall just as sharply” as they have risen [1]. How to read it. A forum of sellers asking for long contracts and coordinated responses is doing its job: it speaks for sellers. Buyers have their own dull machinery: storage, tenders and contracts with more than one seller. A declaration sets a tone. The cargoes and the contract terms set the bill. Nothing here is investment advice.

brent-slips-again-113-88-at-four-in-the-.title: Brent slips again, $113.88 at four in the afternoon
brent-slips-again-113-88-at-four-in-the-.dek: Oil fell for a second session on Tuesday as diplomacy around Tehran continued. The Houthi attacks kept the fall modest.
brent-slips-again-113-88-at-four-in-the-.text: Brent crude futures were down 1.7% at $113.88 a barrel at 16:10 CET on Tuesday, and US WTI 1.7% lower at $100.05, CNBC reports; it was the second falling session in a row [1]. Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei met the country’s top national security official, Mohsen Rezaei, to discuss Tehran’s conditions for ending the war with the United States, and said the state of “neither war nor peace” needs to end, according to a post on his account [1]. Tehran described Monday’s talks with Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani officials as a step towards regional security cooperation, according to the state outlet Tasnim [1]. Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia kept earlier losses limited [1]. Talk lowers the price by a dollar or two; a reopened sea lane would lower it by much more. Nothing here is investment advice.

podium-vs-print-look-through-and-3-8-per.title: Podium vs Print: "look through" and 3.8%
podium-vs-print-look-through-and-3-8-per.dek: Lagarde says the energy shock is too large to look through, but a measured response will do. The September print says prices rise 3.8% a year against a deposit rate of 2.50%. Thursday is about which of the two sentences carries more weight.
podium-vs-print-look-through-and-3-8-per.text: The podium. “The energy shock is too large to ‘look through’ but a measured response remains appropriate to keep inflation in check,” Christine Lagarde told the IMF’s steering committee ten days ago [1]. In the same statement she said long-term interest rates have risen notably since September, and that this “will slow growth and reduce pass-through by more than projected” [1]. The print. Euro-area inflation was 3.8% in September, according to Eurostat’s monthly data, after 3.2% in August and 1.9% in February, the month the war began [2]. The ECB’s deposit rate has gone from 2.00% to 2.50% in two steps, in June and September [5]. The gap. Desk arithmetic: inflation at 3.8% against a deposit rate of 2.50% leaves the real policy rate at about minus 1.3 points. On the face of it, money is still cheap. The president’s answer sits in her own text: the bond market has done part of the work, and wages have “so far shown no material response to the energy shock” [1]. MUFG Research calls the outlook “a more balanced trade-off” and expects a hold on Thursday and a hike in December [3]. Of 32 research houses counted by FinChiefs, all 32 expect a hold [4]. The verdict. Both are true. The print measures what has already happened at the petrol pump and on the heating bill. The podium is about what has not happened yet: higher prices turning into higher wages and then into higher prices again. Core inflation, which leaves out energy and food, is 2.5% [1]. For you, the useful number on Thursday is not the rate, which is expected to stay put, but the sentence after it. Nothing here is investment advice.

the-scenario-said-100-and-75-the-market-.title: The scenario said $100 and €75. The market says $115 and €95
the-scenario-said-100-and-75-the-market-.dek: The ECB's own adverse case for energy has already been overtaken. Previews still expect a hold on Thursday, and the bill for waiting is set in December.
the-scenario-said-100-and-75-the-market-.text: When the ECB drew up its projections in September, its adverse scenario had oil rising to about $100 a barrel and gas to €75 per megawatt hour in the fourth quarter. Current spot prices are about $115 and €95, MUFG Research notes [1]. The bad case has become the base case. And yet: a pause. MUFG expects the deposit rate to stay at 2.50% on Thursday, because sovereign yields rose sharply and financial conditions tightened [1]. “A pause here is reasonable,” writes Henry Cook, who expects a hike in December, when new projections arrive, and another one after that [1]. Markets price about 20 basis points of tightening for December [1]. Economists polled by Reuters see a 70% chance of a December hike [2]. Why wait, if energy is dearer? Because the ECB reacts to energy only if it seeps into everything else. In October’s purchasing managers’ survey, manufacturing input costs accelerated sharply, but services output prices fell back, MUFG says [1]. Household inflation expectations for the medium and long term were unchanged [1]. Desk arithmetic: spot oil is 15% above the adverse scenario, gas about 27% above. For you, that gap shows up on the heating bill before it shows up in any rate decision. Nothing here is investment advice.

the-fed-starts-talking-the-two-year-answ.title: The Fed starts talking, the two-year answers 4.741%
the-fed-starts-talking-the-two-year-answ.dek: Day one of two in Washington. The market prices a hold and listens for December.
the-fed-starts-talking-the-two-year-answ.text: The Federal Reserve’s two-day meeting began on Tuesday, with the decision due on Wednesday. The two-year Treasury yield rose 3 basis points to 4.741%, CNBC reports, and fed funds futures price about a 90% chance that the range stays at 3.75%–4% [1]. Traders are pricing an increase in December, Reuters says [2]. The two-year is the number to watch: it moves with what the market expects the Fed to do next, not with what the Fed says today. Chairman Kevin Warsh’s press conference follows the decision, and investors will parse it for hints on whether the Fed hikes again before the end of the year [1]. The Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, PCE, is due on Thursday [1]. Nothing here is investment advice.

ordinary-ledger-189-of-every-1-000-put-a.title: Ordinary Ledger: €189 of every €1,000 put aside
ordinary-ledger-189-of-every-1-000-put-a.dek: German households saved 18.9% of their disposable income in 2025, well above the EU average of 14.3%. The rate has edged down from 19.6% and held there into 2026.
ordinary-ledger-189-of-every-1-000-put-a.text: Ahead of World Savings Day on 30 and 31 October, the Statistisches Bundesamt has published one number for the household ledger: in 2025 private households in Germany saved 18.9% of their disposable income, against an EU average of 14.3% [1]. Desk arithmetic: of every €1,000 that reached a German household after taxes and transfers, about €189 was put aside; the EU average comes to about €143. The neighbours. French households saved 17.8%, Dutch 17.4%, Austrian 15.7% and Italian 10.8% [1]. Switzerland stood well above at 27.4%, which Destatis puts down to the larger role of private pension saving there; the United States was low at 10.7% [1]. Over the ten years to 2025 German households saved 19.1% of their income on average [1]. The direction. The rate has eased slightly. It was 19.6% in 2024 and 18.9% in both 2025 and the first half of 2026 [1]. The peak came in 2020, at 22.9%, when the pandemic left people consuming less than usual [1]. Desk arithmetic: from 2024 to 2025 the rate fell by 0.7 points, or about €7 less saved per €1,000 of income. Read the small print. This is the gross rate, the measure used for international comparisons. It counts depreciation, mostly on owner-occupied and rented homes, in both saving and income [1]. Price gains or losses on shares and property count as neither [1]. So a rising share price does not make you a better saver in these statistics, and a falling one does not make you a worse one. The net rate, with depreciation deducted, is clearly lower [1]. What the figure does show is a steady habit. Over ten years that included a pandemic and an energy shock, German households put aside 19.1% of their income on average [1]. That habit is the quiet balance sheet behind every bank deposit, pension contract and home loan. It is not glamorous. It is why the system has a cushion. Nothing here is advice.

heating-oil-at-175-and-the-case-for-aski.title: Heating oil at €175, and the case for asking the neighbours
heating-oil-at-175-and-the-case-for-aski.dek: A litre of heating oil cost €1.75 on the German average at midday on Tuesday. Cologne paid €1.80, Nuremberg €1.71.
heating-oil-at-175-and-the-case-for-aski.text: At 11:52 CET on Tuesday, 100 litres of heating oil cost €175.04 on the German average for a 3,000-litre order, up from €173.15 at Monday’s close, according to the price service HeizOel24 [1]. That is about €1.75 a litre [1]. Desk arithmetic: a 3,000-litre tank at that average comes to about €5,251, some €57 more than a day earlier. Where it costs more. Among the large cities, buyers in Cologne paid the most, €1.80 a litre, and buyers in Nuremberg the least, €1.71 [1]. Most Länder got dearer; Bremen and Hesse got slightly cheaper [1]. Desk arithmetic: nine cents a litre between those two cities is about €270 on a 3,000-litre order. Why the bill is sticky. Transport keeps the bill high even when crude eases. The International Energy Agency reported that crude bound for Asia cost on average $93 a barrel at loading in October but $131 delivered, HeizOel24 notes, and such freight costs can keep diesel and heating oil dear in Europe even when Brent falls [1]. Austria paid €185.76 per 100 litres, Switzerland 178.46 francs [1]. The dull tip that works. If you only need a small amount, HeizOel24 suggests joining neighbours in a collective order [1]. One lorry, one trip, several tanks: the delivery cost is shared. Comparing three quotes on the same morning costs a few minutes. Nothing here is advice.

saarland-s-bin-bill-about-ten-euros-more.title: Saarland's bin bill: about ten euros more
saarland-s-bin-bill-about-ten-euros-more.dek: The Entsorgungsverband Saar proposes raising waste fees by almost 8% in each of 2027 and 2028. Wastewater rises 2.5%.
saarland-s-bin-bill-about-ten-euros-more.text: The Entsorgungsverband Saar, which handles waste and wastewater for Saarland households, plans to raise waste fees by almost 8% in both 2027 and 2028, Saarländischer Rundfunk reports [1]. The managing director, Holger Schmitt, cites the carbon price, pay rises for refuse workers and higher logistics costs [1]. For an average household with a 120-litre bin emptied ten times a year, that means almost €10 more next year and almost €11 more in 2028 [1]. The wastewater fee rises 2.5%, about 36 cents a head a month, or roughly €4.50 a year [1]. These are proposals: the municipal councils vote, and the result is due at the association’s assembly in December [1]. A fee rise that passes through elected councils, with the reasons on the table, is how a public service should send its bill.

the-suppliers-buy-a-slice-of-the-custome.title: The suppliers buy a slice of the customer
the-suppliers-buy-a-slice-of-the-custome.dek: Nvidia will put $3 billion and AMD $1 billion into Meta's share offering. When the chip makers fund the buyer of their chips, read the order book and the cheque together.
the-suppliers-buy-a-slice-of-the-custome.text: This morning’s tech note was about a chip maker standing behind the value of its own hardware. By mid-morning there was a second variation on the theme. Nvidia said on Tuesday it will invest $3 billion in Meta’s equity offering, and AMD announced $1 billion, CNBC reports [1]. The offering. On Monday Meta said it wants to raise $95 billion for AI infrastructure: $35 billion first, through underwritten public share offerings, then another $60 billion through an at-the-market programme [1]. Meta’s announcement said Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom were interested in buying up to $5 billion of the shares [1]. Desk arithmetic: the two confirmed stakes come to $4 billion, about 4% of the total Meta wants to raise, and about 11% of the first $35 billion. What comes with the cheque. Nvidia said Meta would expand its deployment of Vera Rubin systems and Vera processors, and that the two would deepen work on Muse, Meta’s AI agent [1]. AMD said its Helios racks were running at Meta and its EPYC processors powered Muse [1]. So the money and the orders travel together. That is not improper; it is common in industries where supplier and customer need each other for years. It does mean you should read a supplier’s sales figures with its investment portfolio open beside them. A habit, not a one-off. Nvidia has invested in OpenAI, Anthropic, Intel and xAI, and has taken part in 121 investment rounds so far this year, up from 13 in 2022, according to Dealroom data cited by CNBC [1]. AMD has been in 25 rounds this year, against two in 2022 [1]. Desk arithmetic: Nvidia’s count is more than nine times what it was four years ago. The market’s verdict on Tuesday was mild: AMD up 3%, Nvidia flat, Meta down 1% [1]. That calm is the right register. Vendor finance is old machinery, used for aircraft, ships and telephone networks. It works best when everyone can see who owes what to whom, which is why this week’s earnings filings matter more than this week’s press releases. Nothing here is investment advice.

a-laptop-with-a-bill-of-materials-you-ca.title: A laptop with a bill of materials you can audit
a-laptop-with-a-bill-of-materials-you-ca.dek: Anduril and Qualcomm announced BlueChip, a rugged laptop with about 90% of its components from the US or allied countries. The display is still a problem.
a-laptop-with-a-bill-of-materials-you-ca.text: The defence company Anduril and the chip designer Qualcomm announced a computer called BlueChip on Tuesday, TechCrunch reports [1]. The first model is a hardened laptop for the military, government agencies, first responders and police; preorders open in 2027 [1]. The selling point is the list. About 90% of the components in the first generation come from the US or allied countries, including the processor, a Snapdragon X Series chip built at TSMC’s new facility in Arizona [1]. “We have a technical roadmap to get to 100% domestic over time,” said Anduril’s founder, Palmer Luckey [1]. He named the display as one of several parts that, by his account, are still made only in China; he has found an American supplier for the cover glass [1]. The honest price tag. No price yet, but Luckey estimates about 20% above typical high-end PCs [1]. He was candid about the consumer case: an ordinary buyer without a particular need would be “better off buying a Dell laptop” [1]. Rugged computers are already about a $5 billion market, according to TechCrunch [1]. Why it matters beyond the barracks. Government buyers face rules that require them to buy US-made computers, and the pitch here is a supply chain the customer can track and audit [1]. That is a procurement story more than a gadget story. An auditable bill of materials is dull paperwork, and it is exactly what security buyers have lacked. Whether the last 10% can be made at home is a question of factories, not slogans. Nothing here is investment advice.

opera-puts-the-model-in-the-browser.title: Opera puts the model in the browser
opera-puts-the-model-in-the-browser.dek: WebAI, a proposed standard from Opera, lets websites use open-weight AI models running on your own computer. It is opt-in.
opera-puts-the-model-in-the-browser.text: Opera has introduced WebAI, a new web standard that lets AI models run directly in the browser rather than in the cloud, TechCrunch reports [1]. It works with open-weight models such as Google’s Gemma and, on Macs, Apple’s on-device foundation model [1]. An early preview is in Opera One, with Opera GX and Opera Neon to follow; users must opt in [1]. “Users don’t need AI subscriptions, the information the local AI handles stays on their own device,” the company said [1]. The trade-off is your own hardware: performance depends on the machine [1]. A model on your own disk is less exciting than one in a data centre. It is also one fewer place your text has to travel.

48-000-warnings-35-responses-europe-s-he.title: 48,000 warnings, 35 responses: Europe's health report card in one speech
48-000-warnings-35-responses-europe-s-he.dek: WHO Europe opened its annual meeting in Copenhagen with the numbers that rarely make headlines. Most of them are about routine done well, and some are about gaps.
48-000-warnings-35-responses-europe-s-he.text: Speeches at international meetings are usually skipped, and usually rightly. Tuesday’s opening address at WHO Europe’s Regional Committee in Copenhagen is worth reading for its numbers, not its rhetoric [1]. Corinne Capuano, the officer-in-charge of the regional office, delivered it while Regional Director Hans Kluge is on special leave, after what she called “a year of hard change”, with staff leaving in a reorganisation [1]. Start with the dull machinery. Between January and October, the region’s teams analysed 48,000 pieces of information on possible health threats; 35 needed an operational response [1]. Desk arithmetic: about one in 1,400, and 47,965 that did not need one. This year’s responses included a hantavirus outbreak on a cruise ship in May, dengue and West Nile virus in the summer, and the first documented human infection with Shamonda virus [1]. For the first time, every state in the region filed its annual report under the International Health Regulations, and the region now has 38 classified emergency medical teams [1]. A sorting office that reads every letter and acts on a few is doing its job. The routine wins are larger than they sound. Across the region, 91% of children get all three doses of the diphtheria, tetanus and whooping-cough vaccine, measles cases fell by 75% in 2025 compared with 2024, and 92% of countries have introduced HPV vaccination [1]. Latvia restricted alcohol availability and alcohol-related deaths fell significantly within five months, she said [1]. The gaps were stated just as plainly. One in five tuberculosis cases goes undiagnosed or unreported, half of HIV diagnoses come too late, and HIV deaths are rising [1]. WHO Europe’s analysis counts 1.8 million deaths among people under 75 that prevention or treatment could avoid [1]. A quarter of children aged 7 to 9 are overweight or living with obesity, based on data from 37 countries [1]. The workforce line deserves the most attention. Women make up 77% of the health workforce yet earn on average up to 28% less per month than men, and nursing and carer shortages hit hardest in rural areas and smaller countries [1]. Women in the region also spend 81.3% of their lives in good health against 83.5% for men, which means more demand for long-term care from a workforce already short of people [1]. If you want to know where Europe’s health systems will strain, you do not need a forecast. You need the payroll.

a-hospital-switched-off-its-computers-an.title: A hospital switched off its computers, and the ambulances went next door
a-hospital-switched-off-its-computers-an.dek: A cyberattack shut clinics at New Mexico's only Level 1 trauma centre on Monday. By the evening, the hospitals were open again.
a-hospital-switched-off-its-computers-an.text: On Monday, the University of New Mexico’s health system in Albuquerque detected a network breach at around 11:30 local time (18:30 CET), according to a message to staff reported by the university’s student newspaper [1]. About 40 minutes later, staff were asked to shut down and unplug computers and turn off Wi-Fi on mobile devices [1]. The system runs the state’s largest teaching hospital and its only Level 1 trauma centre [1]. By 14:30 local time (21:30 CET) it was diverting ambulances to other hospitals and had cancelled all clinic appointments for the day [1]. A few hours later it said systems were coming back in phases; a final update that day said all its hospitals were open and clinics would resume Tuesday’s appointments and procedures [1]. Tuesday’s classes at the medical, nursing and pharmacy schools were cancelled [1]. An extortion group called BYOD has claimed the attack and says it stole student and employee data, including US social security numbers; those claims are unconfirmed [1]. Because it is an active law-enforcement investigation, the university said it is “limited in what we can share” [1]. Two details are the real news for patients. Ambulances had somewhere to go: the university thanked “the health systems in Albuquerque and Santa Fe” that took its patients [1]. And the hospitals were open again within a day [1]. Pulling the plug quickly, diverting cleanly and restoring in phases is not luck. It is a drill someone practised.

sepsis-joins-the-readmission-ledger.title: Sepsis joins the readmission ledger
sepsis-joins-the-readmission-ledger.dek: US hospitals will be penalised for sepsis patients who come back within 30 days, from fiscal 2030. The countdown starts with confidential reports.
sepsis-joins-the-readmission-ledger.text: The US Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has added a 30-day, all-cause readmission rate after sepsis to its Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program, the seventh condition on the list; it covers Medicare patients aged 65 and over [1]. Hospitals get confidential early-look reports for the 2028 and 2029 programme years; financial penalties start in fiscal 2030 [1]. Studies show that about a quarter of sepsis survivors are readmitted within 30 days, with a median of 11 days [1]. Because the measure counts every unplanned return, a return with heart failure or a drug side effect counts as much as a relapse [1]. The advice from clinicians is plain: plan discharge from day one, check the infection is actually cleared, and tell patients which symptoms mean “call” and which mean “come in” [1]. One nurse noted that patients’ toothbrushes often stay in the wrapper; brushing helps prevent pneumonia [1]. A penalty is crude. A checklist with a toothbrush on it is not.

one-call-from-helsinki-two-readouts.title: One call from Helsinki, two readouts
one-call-from-helsinki-two-readouts.dek: Finland's president and Norway's prime minister phoned Vladimir Putin on Tuesday. Both sides published accounts. They agree on the Abu Dhabi talks and the phone line, and on little else.
one-call-from-helsinki-two-readouts.text: Alexander Stubb and Jonas Gahr Støre spoke to Vladimir Putin by telephone from Helsinki on Tuesday [1]. Norway’s government said the call followed the two leaders’ meeting in Oslo on 20 October, was held “in consultation with Ukraine” and was meant to convey messages directly to Putin about the coming negotiations in Abu Dhabi [1]. The Kremlin said the call came at the Finnish and Norwegian request [2]. Where the accounts agree. Both sides tie the call to Abu Dhabi. The Kremlin wrote that the three “welcomed the agreement to resume trilateral talks” between Russia, Ukraine and the United States there in early to mid-November [2]. Both mention security in the Baltic Sea and the north; the Kremlin’s version adds that the two Nordic leaders stressed “international maritime law and the freedom of navigation” [2]. And the Kremlin records that the three agreed to keep in direct telephone contact [2]. Where they do not. The Nordic text stresses what it was not: Stubb and Støre “did not speak on the behalf of Europe as a whole,” and they repeated their support for Ukraine [1]. “Ending the war requires direct discussions,” Stubb said; Støre spoke of “enormous human and material costs” and of de-escalation [1]. The Kremlin text instead has Putin restating the war’s “root causes” and saying a lasting peace requires Russia’s interests to be considered “in full and without any conditions attached,” while blaming EU and NATO policy for prolonging the fighting [2]. The Kremlin also used the call to announce something concrete: a US-mediated humanitarian operation under way near Oleshky, with a temporary ceasefire in the Kherson sector [2]. Reuters reported that Ukraine’s human rights commissioner confirmed Kyiv was honouring the halt, even as strikes continued elsewhere, including on Kyiv overnight [3]. Two neighbours with long borders opened a channel without claiming a mandate they do not have, and agreed to keep it open. That is modest. Modest channels are how the larger ones get built.

raf-fairford-two-charges-under-the-2023-.title: RAF Fairford: two charges under the 2023 Act
raf-fairford-two-charges-under-the-2023-.dek: Prosecutors charged two London men after a police investigation into an incident at the Gloucestershire airbase. Police believe the foreign intelligence service involved is Iran's.
raf-fairford-two-charges-under-the-2023-.text: The Crown Prosecution Service said on Tuesday that two men, both 24 and from Westminster, London, have been charged under the National Security Act 2023 after a Counter Terrorism Policing investigation into an incident involving RAF Fairford [1]. Mohmed Abdulkarim is charged with conduct likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service between 31 August and 28 September [1]. Nouman Essghir is charged with being in the vicinity of a prohibited place on 22 August for a purpose prejudicial to the UK [1]. Both were due at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on Tuesday [1]. Counter Terrorism Policing said it believes the intelligence service involved is Iran’s [2]. Its head, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, said police had seen “a range of incidents in recent months” they believe were directed by the Iranian state, and asked the public to report anything that worries them [2]. A third man, a 25-year-old UK-Iranian dual national, was released without charge but remains on police bail, as do five other men [2]. The CPS was explicit about what a charge is and is not. Its decision is “not in any sense a finding of, or implication of, any guilt”, and it asked that nothing be reported or shared that could prejudice the proceedings [1]. So this desk stops here. The useful point is procedural: the 2023 Act’s offences are now being put before a court, which is where its definitions will be tested.

sanaa-calls-cairo-s-vote-a-declaration-o.title: Sanaa calls Cairo's vote a declaration of war
sanaa-calls-cairo-s-vote-a-declaration-o.dek: A Houthi leader answered Egypt's parliamentary authorisation to help defend Saudi Arabia, on the day after a de-escalation mission to Tehran.
sanaa-calls-cairo-s-vote-a-declaration-o.text: Mohammed Ali al-Houthi, a member of the Houthis’ political bureau, said on Tuesday that the Egyptian parliament’s decision to authorise military support for Saudi Arabia amounted to declaring “war against the Republic of Yemen” [1]. His Telegram statement mostly answered Monday’s visit to Tehran by the Saudi defence minister, Pakistan’s army chief and Türkiye’s intelligence chief, who met Iranian leaders to try to de-escalate [1]. He said the group was “not afraid of any alliance” [1]. Since the Houthis stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia this month, neither Pakistan nor Türkiye, Riyadh’s partners in the Mecca defence pact, has announced strikes on the group [1]. For now the words are louder than the orders, and the diplomats are still travelling.

five-indian-states-have-now-declared-dro.title: Five Indian states have now declared drought, and the rain gauge tells you when it stopped
five-indian-states-have-now-declared-dro.dek: Rajasthan and Gujarat joined Karnataka, Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh. The relief comes as cattle camps and paused loan collections, the unglamorous kind.
five-indian-states-have-now-declared-dro.text: India’s drought map grew on Tuesday. Rajasthan has declared drought in 80 tehsils (sub-districts) across 14 districts, and Gujarat in four districts: Kutch, Devbhumi Dwarka, Jamnagar and Porbandar [1]. They follow Karnataka, Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh [1]. Karnataka’s government says its latest estimates put 80% of the kharif crop, the monsoon-season harvest, as destroyed [1]. In Rajasthan, Jodhpur has the most drought-hit tehsils at 12, followed by Barmer and Jalore with 10 each [1]. Of the 80, 69 are classed as severely and 11 as moderately hit [1]. Bajra, jowar, moong, moth beans and sesame have been lost, and Jodhpur’s water storage stood at 15.15% on 16 October [1]. The season total alone would not tell you this. A modelled grid point over Jodhpur shows 257.1 mm of rain since 1 June, against a 1991–2020 average of 277.5 mm for the same days [2]. Desk arithmetic: about 7% short, hardly a catastrophe on paper. The shape is the story. By 15 August the grid point was ahead of normal at 231.6 mm; from 16 August to 26 October it recorded 25.5 mm, against an average of 80.1 mm [2]. Desk arithmetic: about a third of the usual late-season rain. One grid point is not a district, and model grids smooth out local storms, so read it as a shape, not a measurement. What a declaration buys is dull and useful. Rajasthan has announced cattle camps in affected areas and a six-month suspension of farm-loan recovery [1]. Gujarat says it has been selling fodder at cheaper rates since July [1]. None of that makes rain. It does stop a bad season from turning into a forced sale of the herd or a defaulted loan, which is how one dry autumn becomes three poor years. If you buy Indian rice, pulses or spices, nothing in Tuesday’s reports puts a number on prices, and the desk will not invent one. The quieter point is for anyone who thinks of climate as an averages problem: farms live on timing, and a month’s rain arriving early is not the same as a month’s rain.

michigan-s-fires-may-sleep-under-the-sno.title: Michigan's fires may sleep under the snow
michigan-s-fires-may-sleep-under-the-sno.dek: Three wildfires in the Upper Peninsula have burned into the forest floor. Officials say only soaking rain or heavy, wet snow will put them out.
michigan-s-fires-may-sleep-under-the-sno.text: Wildfire season in Michigan usually means spring, after the snow melts and before the leaves come out [1]. This year it is late October, and the worry is the coming spring too. At least three large wildfires have been burning in the state’s Upper Peninsula since early October, covering about 1,400 acres, and they remain only partially contained [1]. Desk arithmetic: about 570 hectares. Lingering drought has let embers burn several feet down into the duff, the layers of decaying plant matter on the forest floor [1]. Officials fear the fires could smoulder through winter and flare up again in spring, like the “zombie fires” of Alaska’s and Canada’s peatlands [1]. “At this point in time, I wouldn’t count it out,” said Keith Murphy, the state natural-resources department’s protection manager for the region [1]. “Usually, we have the droughty August and we run into deep burning, but it’s just continued on through October now,” he said [1]. Only saturated soil will finish the job, and Murphy said heavy, wet snow would do more than light, fluffy lake-effect snow [1]. There is precedent, and it is not frightening. A peat fire in Allegan County smouldered for nearly a year before it was put out in autumn 2013, and the 1976 Seney fire, which burned eight feet into peat, was finally put out by melting snow the next spring [1]. The useful part is the plan: officials will monitor how rain and snow affect the fire sites in the coming months [1]. Fire crews who keep watching a fire nobody can see are the adaptation story.

the-soybeans-caught-up-the-corn-is-still.title: The soybeans caught up; the corn is still in the field
the-soybeans-caught-up-the-corn-is-still.dek: USDA's weekly count: soybeans 79% harvested, ahead of normal; corn 60%, behind. The week's weather should mostly let the combines run.
the-soybeans-caught-up-the-corn-is-still.text: America’s harvest is a weather story told in percentages. By Sunday, 79% of US soybeans were harvested, two points ahead of the five-year average of 77%, after a very late start in September [1]. Corn was 60% harvested, six points behind the average of 66%; in Iowa, the largest producer, only 47% is in, against a usual 67% [1]. Of the corn still standing, 56% is rated good to excellent [1]. DTN’s meteorologist expects scattered showers and mostly above-normal temperatures this week, with “minor” disruptions to fieldwork and possible tropical moisture reaching Texas on Friday [1]. Nobody in that report is predicting a shortage. They are predicting a lot of long days on a combine.

de-lignite-27pm.title: Lignite took the storm weekend off, then went back to work
de-lignite-27pm.subtitle: Electricity generated from lignite in Germany, realised, daily total, MWh
de-lignite-27pm.source: Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de, realised generation from lignite, Germany (filter 1223), days 1 Sep to 26 Oct 2026, retrieved 27 Oct 2026 · CC BY 4.0
de-lignite-27pm.alt: Line chart of daily electricity generation from lignite in Germany from 1 September to 26 October 2026, in megawatt hours. It averages about 197,771 MWh a day in September and peaks at 291,434 MWh on 2 October. It stands at 255,448 MWh on Wednesday 21 October, drops to 54,346 MWh on storm Saturday 24 October, the lowest day since 14 June 2026, and 62,470 MWh on Sunday 25 October, then climbs back to 162,086 MWh on Monday 26 October, the latest value.

ea-hicp-dfr-27pm.title: Prices ran ahead, the rate walked behind
ea-hicp-dfr-27pm.subtitle: Euro-area HICP inflation, annual change, %, monthly · ECB deposit facility rate, %, month-end
ea-hicp-dfr-27pm.source: Eurostat prc_hicp_minr (CC BY 4.0) · ECB Data Portal FM.D.U2.EUR.4F.KR.DFR.LEV · retrieved 27 Oct 2026 · latest inflation value September 2026
ea-hicp-dfr-27pm.alt: Line chart since January 2025 of euro-area HICP inflation and the ECB deposit rate. Inflation is 2.5% in January 2025, between 1.9% and 2.2% for the rest of 2025, 1.7% in January 2026 and 1.9% in February, then rises after the energy shock to 3.2% in May, 2.8% in June and 3.8% in September 2026, the latest value. The deposit rate falls from 3.00% to 2.00% by mid-2025, rises to 2.25% in June 2026 and to 2.50% in September 2026, where it stands in October 2026. The ECB decides on 29 October.

jodhpur-rain-27pm.title: Wet until mid-August, then almost nothing
jodhpur-rain-27pm.subtitle: Rain since 1 June, running total, mm · Jodhpur grid point (modelled), 2026 vs 1991–2020 average for the same days
jodhpur-rain-27pm.source: Open-Meteo Historical Weather API (open-meteo.com), daily precipitation at 26.29°N 73.02°E; 2026 from its default reanalysis/analysis blend, 1991–2020 average from ERA5 (Copernicus/ECMWF); desk running totals at weekly points; retrieved 27 Oct 2026 · Open-Meteo data CC BY 4.0. Modelled grid values for one point, not station readings or a district average.
jodhpur-rain-27pm.alt: Line chart of modelled rainfall at a Jodhpur grid point, running total from 1 June. In 2026 the total runs slightly below the 1991–2020 average through July, pulls ahead in early August to 231.6 mm by 15 August, then adds only 25.5 mm more, ending at 257.1 mm on Monday 26 October 2026, the latest value. The 1991–2020 average for the same days keeps climbing to 277.5 mm by 26 October.

israel-turnout-27pm.title: Ahead of 2022 at every hour
israel-turnout-27pm.subtitle: Israel, Knesset election turnout reported by the Central Elections Committee, % of eligible voters by the hour shown, 2022 and 27 Oct 2026
israel-turnout-27pm.source: Israel Central Elections Committee turnout readings (local time, CET+1), as reported by The Times of Israel, Israel Hayom and thestateofisrael.com, retrieved 27 Oct 2026 · polls close 22:00 local; final turnout not yet known
israel-turnout-27pm.alt: Bar chart of Israeli election turnout by the hour, 2022 against 27 October 2026. By 10:00 local time it was 15.9% in 2022 and 16.68% in 2026; by 12:00, 28.4% and 31.5%; by 14:00, 38.9% and 44.9%; by 16:00, 47.5% in 2022 and 55.7% in 2026, the latest reading.
